newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders, euro pact agreed, turn to east Europe.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders, euro pact agreed, turn to east Europe.

text.p: European Union leaders, having clinched a landmark deal for their planned single currency, turn to the rest of the future on Saturday as they meet counterparts from 11 countries clamouring to join.
Enlargement and a joint attack on crime and drugs were set to take centre stage as the leaders of the 15-nation bloc began the final day of their end-of-year summit.
The heads of state and government were to meet counterparts from Poland, Hungary, the Czech republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Romania and Cyprus.
All have been promised they can join the Union some time in the near future. Formal negotiations are due to begin about a year from now, six months after the EU finishes rewriting its treaty.
Irish officials admitted the discussions might be an anti-climax after the accord reached on Friday on a pact to keep government budgets sound after the euro is introduced on January 1, 1999.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said the pact, which broke a Franco-German standoff on economic and monetary union (EMU), showed EU leaders had "the political will to make the project work."
Draft conclusions from the summit, to be approved later on Saturday, urged EU institutions, public bodies and financial markets to intensify their preparations for the euro.
Designs for the new euro bills were unveiled on Friday, a literally graphic display of the bloc's fervent intention to see the project through.

British Prime Minister John Major has sounded the lone dissenting note at the summit, reiterating on Saturday morning his doubts about whether the single currency would be launched on time in January 1999 despite what he called the Herculean efforts of its supporters.

"If it goes wrong because people go in because it is their political will to do so when it is not economically sensible ...then the damage right across Europe will be very serious indeed," Major told BBC radio in an interview.

Major also gave notice that Britain would oppose many of the proposals others support in the inter-governmental conference (IGC), the negotiations for the new treaty destined to be approved at a summit in Amsterdam in June next year.
Major argued against a more integrated Europe, against countries losing veto rights and against proposed provisions to allow some member states to integrate more quickly than others.
He also scorned the idea of putting an employment chapter in the EU treaty to make job creation a top priority in EU matters.

A declaration on employment by the summit aims to coordinate an EU attack on joblessness through better training and heightened adaptability to stave off the threat of more jobs seeping towards east Asian states and Pacific Rim countries.
The summit's key achievement, however, was to hammer out the post-euro stability pact in a way that was deemed strong enough to satisfy Germany the euro will be as hard as its deutschemark.

Under the deal, countries will be exempted from penalties for running up deficits of more than three per cent of gross domestic product if their economies went into recession by two percent in a year.

Any fine will have to be agreed by EU leaders if a member's economy shrinks by more than 0.75 percent of GDP. This was a nod towards France, which wanted the fines to be subject to a political decision rather than accounting practices.

Germany, which had argued for automatic sanctions for overspending, was satisfied. Asked whether the euro would be as solid as the deutschemark, German Finance Minister Theo Wiagel replied: "Jawohl (Yes, certainly)".
